records.name: RNA-lipoplex
records.tldr: An RNA-lipoplex is a particle in which RNA is complexed with lipids. Its behaviour depends on the exact lipids, charge balance and route, so a result for one lipoplex does not transfer to another product.
records.summary:
RNA carries negative charge, and positively charged lipid components can associate with it. RNA-lipoplex names a family of formulations, and the final particle need not be positively charged: net charge depends on the balance of RNA and lipid, the ingredients and the preparation. The naming overlaps with lipid nanoparticles, so the actual composition and properties matter more than the acronym.

In one study of the approach, intravenous RNA-lipoplexes were aimed at dendritic cells by adjusting net charge, without adding a molecular ligand; the particles protected RNA from ribonucleases, were taken up and expressed in dendritic cells and macrophages in lymphoid compartments, and triggered interferon-alpha release from plasmacytoid dendritic cells and macrophages, with antigen-specific T-cell responses and tumour rejection in the authors' in vivo experiments (Kranz and colleagues; the abstract also reports a phase I trial in which three people with melanoma had been treated at a low dose when it was published). An innate-immune signal is not antigen expression, antigen-specific immunity or clinical benefit.

The pancreatic cancer vaccine autogene cevumeran shows how specific a lipoplex product is. In the phase I trial each patient's vaccine held two uridine mRNA strands, each encoding up to 10 neoepitopes, formulated in lipoplex nanoparticles of about 400 nm made from the cationic lipid DOTMA and the phospholipid DOPE, given intravenously (Rojas and colleagues, methods). That trial gave atezolizumab and the vaccine to 16 people and then a modified FOLFIRINOX regimen to 15, so it describes one product within a treatment sequence and neither ranks lipoplexes against lipid nanoparticles nor isolates the vaccine's effect.

A commercial cationic-lipid lipoplex reagent shows how far charge and properties can vary. In vitro, eGFP mRNA lipoplexes formed in pure water measured 98.7 to 121.5 nm by dynamic light scattering and had zeta potentials from -14.4 to -58.7 mV across reagent lots, so a cationic lipid does not guarantee a positive particle, and the value was measured for that preparation, medium and lot (Appelbaum and colleagues; canine retina and cell lines, no cancer setting). The same study separates uptake from expression: after subretinal injection eGFP mRNA was detected in all retinal cell types but protein was limited to the retinal pigment epithelium. A product with the same antigen sequence but different lipids or route is not the same product: particle size and route changed where mRNA LNPs went in mice (Di and colleagues), and the Rojas product is described by its own composition, route and protocol.

For messenger RNA, being inside an endosome is not enough: it must reach the cytosol to be translated. The endosomal-release experiments summarised under lipid nanoparticles used LNPs, not lipoplexes, so they do not by themselves describe a lipoplex.

notes: Appelbaum and colleagues measured RNA complexation by gel electrophoresis separately from light-scattering size and zeta potential in stated media and reagent lots. Report the assay and denominator behind any complexed or encapsulated fraction, and assess RNA integrity separately. These product measurements do not establish cytosolic release or expression. In a vaccine, expression in an antigen-presenting cell is also an earlier observation than peptide display, antigen-specific recognition or tumour control.

Multiple RNAs raise separate questions: whether RNA products are mixed, whether RNAs share a formulation, whether individual particles carry both, and whether the same cells express both proteins. Zhang and colleagues used Lipofectamine 2000 to compare premixed eGFP and mCherry RNAs with mixtures of single-RNA lipoplexes. In HeLa cells, the mixture could match the population-average ratio while individual cells showed variable uptake and expression; joint formulation improved the single-cell correspondence. Mouse embryonic-stem-cell-derived retinal organoids and zebrafish embryo hindbrain injections showed the same qualitative contrast. Input ratios were RNA mass ratios, and reporter fluorescence was measured separately from labelled-RNA uptake. The reporters differed in detection and/or expression. Average strand loading and assumed even mixing do not establish every particle's cargo, and fluorescence ratios do not by themselves specify absolute protein molar ratios or functional assembly. This study of reporters and a research reagent does not establish that every carrier or therapeutic RNA mixture behaves the same.

In a different comparison, Chen and colleagues attached DOTAP/DOPE lipoplexes carrying one mCherry reporter to polymer microbubbles or gave the lipoplexes beside the bubbles. They tested 4T1 cells and intravenously treated female BALB/c mice with subcutaneous 4T1 tumours, six per group. With ultrasound, separate administration gave greater reporter-positive tumour area and signal farther from vessels; attachment favoured vascular and perivascular signal and was more ultrasound dependent in the cell-culture comparison. Tissue percentages measured fluorescent image area, not the fraction of all tumour cells, and distances over 50 micrometres were excluded from the vessel analysis. Off-site signal was lower in spleen with attachment, while liver differences were not statistically significant. This compares a physical delivery assembly, not whether two RNAs enter the same cell; reporter expression does not demonstrate cancer control or clinical safety.

records.name: Lipid nanoparticles for RNA delivery
records.tldr: A lipid nanoparticle is a formulated fat-based carrier that protects RNA and helps it enter cells. Getting into a cell, releasing usable RNA into the cell fluid and making protein are separate steps, and a particle can succeed at the first without the others.
records.summary:
A typical RNA-delivery lipid nanoparticle combines an ionisable lipid, a phospholipid, cholesterol and a polyethylene glycol lipid around the RNA; the proportions, lipid identities and preparation change behaviour, so the label LNP alone does not name a product. Ionisable lipids change charge with pH. In common designs they are more protonated in an acidic environment and less charged at physiological pH; the extent depends on the lipid and its environment. This can support membrane interactions during endosomal escape, whose performance remains formulation- and cell-dependent (Hou and colleagues, review). Cells usually take particles into endosomes, and messenger RNA is translated by ribosomes in the cytosol, so usable delivery needs the RNA to leave the endosome. Ordinary messenger RNA does not need to enter the nucleus.

Uptake and expression were measured separately in primary human adipocytes, fibroblasts and HeLa cells with six LNP formulations of similar size (54 to 73 nm) carrying eGFP mRNA: total uptake was necessary but not a sufficient predictor of delivery, one formulation gave the highest eGFP expression despite moderate uptake, prolonged uptake impaired endosomal acidification and left mRNA in compartments unproductive for delivery, and early endocytic and recycling compartments had the highest probability of escape (Paramasivam and colleagues). In that study eGFP expression served as a proxy for release; it did not measure the fraction of RNA that escaped.

Where particles go depends on formulation and route. In female BALB/c mice given luciferase-mRNA LNPs by intramuscular, subcutaneous or intravenous injection, some intramuscular particles reached the liver and spleen, smaller particles more than larger ones, bigger particles tended to stay at the injection site, and liver expression was the most prominent; exposure and expression were not linearly related (Di and colleagues). Mouse distribution is not another product's distribution in people, and local injection does not establish local delivery. Readouts answer different questions: particle size, RNA integrity and encapsulated fraction describe the product; a labelled lipid or labelled RNA shows where a label went, not that intact RNA arrived or was released; and protein per identified live cell shows expression. In the mouse study a lipid label (DiR or deuterium-labelled cholesterol) and luciferase activity were measured separately and did not track each other linearly, and every figure needs its denominator (all cells, live cells or expressing cells). Uptake and protein are different fractions: in the six-formulation study the formulation with the highest eGFP expression had only moderate uptake, so a formulation that takes up in more cells can still make protein in fewer. Message and effect also run on separate clocks: in cultured mouse T cells CAR expression from LNP mRNA peaked at 24 hours and fell over the next days (Rurik and colleagues), and the same RNA in particles of different size or by a different route distributed differently, so the same RNA is not the same product.

The cancer relevance is as a carrier of antigen-encoding RNA or of instructions for engineering immune cells. The carrier, where it goes, which cells make protein and what that protein does are different questions; none of these studies is evidence of clinical benefit.

notes: In an invented comparison using 100 identified live cells per formulation at the same measurement time, A shows uptake in 70 cells and encoded protein in 10; B shows uptake in 40 and protein in 25. Uptake is therefore 70 versus 40 per cent, while protein expression is 10 versus 25 per cent on the same live-cell denominator. These separate counts do not show which cells had both signals, the fraction of intact RNA that escaped, the amount of protein per cell or a biological effect. Name the cargo, cell population, assay, timing and controls before comparing formulations; a brighter carrier signal alone does not establish usable RNA delivery.

records.name: Targeted lipid nanoparticles
records.tldr: Targeted lipid nanoparticles use a surface ligand or a changed lipid mix to favour particular cells or organs. Enrichment in a tissue is not the same as working protein made only in the intended cell type.
records.summary:
Two strategies are separate. A ligand strategy adds a binding molecule such as an antibody to the particle surface so it recognises a marker on intended cells; binding must still lead to uptake and usable release, and the marker may sit on other cells. A formulation strategy changes the lipids: selective organ targeting (SORT) added a supplemental lipid to otherwise standard LNPs and, after intravenous injection in mice, shifted delivery toward lung, spleen or liver; with a Cre reporter, the lung formulation edited about 40 per cent of epithelial and 65 per cent of endothelial cells, the spleen formulation 12 per cent of B cells and 10 per cent of T cells, and the liver formulation 93 per cent of hepatocytes (Cheng and colleagues, as reported). These are measured results in mice, not a rule connecting a composition to an organ in people.

A CD5-directed example shows both the aim and its limit. CD5-targeted LNPs carrying modified mRNA for a chimeric antigen receptor against fibroblast activation protein were tested in activated mouse T cells in culture (81 per cent expressed a GFP reporter and 83 per cent the receptor, against 7 per cent with isotype-control antibody particles) and then injected intravenously into mice with angiotensin II and phenylephrine induced cardiac injury. Receptor expression appeared in each major T-cell subset by flow cytometry (87 per cent of receptor-positive T cells were CD4-positive), bioluminescence showed spleen targeting only with CD5 particles, and liver expression occurred with both CD5 and control particles, so an organ-level signal and the identity of the expressing cells were measured separately; treatment reduced fibrosis and restored cardiac function in these mice (Rurik and colleagues, author manuscript). The delivery address was CD5 and the encoded receptor recognised a different target. This was a fibrosis model, not a cancer trial, and the authors disclose patents on the platforms.

A later study used targeted LNPs to deliver mRNA to specific T-cell subsets; its abstract reports reprogrammed CD8-positive T cells in samples from healthy donors and people with autoimmune disease, tumour control in humanised mice and B-cell depletion in cynomolgus monkeys (Hunter and colleagues; abstract only, full text not retrievable). Each of those is a different experiment in a different setting, and none is evidence of benefit against solid tumours in people.

Enrichment is not exclusivity. In a Cre-reporter experiment recombination appeared in 81.1 per cent of CD4-positive and 75.6 per cent of CD8-positive splenocytes but also in 15.0 per cent of CD3-negative cells, mainly B cells, dendritic cells and macrophages (Rurik and colleagues), and the 87 per cent figure above is a share of receptor-positive cells, not the share of CD4 T cells that expressed the receptor, so the denominator matters. Cargo type also matters for how long the effect lasts: RNA encoding a receptor produced transient CAR T cells in that study, whereas RNA encoding a genome editor can leave a lasting DNA change, as when SORT lipid nanoparticles delivered Cas9 mRNA and guide RNA to edit cells in mice (Cheng and colleagues) and Cas9 mRNA with an AAV repair template knocked a CAR into T cells in culture (Eyquem and colleagues).

Organ signal, cell identity, protein function and clinical effect need separate measurements, with matched untargeted controls and identified intended and unintended recipient populations.

Report particle or cargo amount per stated tissue quantity separately from protein amount or the protein-positive fraction within each identified live-cell subset. Include intended and unintended recipient populations, matched controls, route and sampling time; an organ-level signal cannot identify every expressing cell.
